stories.title: Autoresearch: The feedback loop behind self-improving agents
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Introspection co-founder Roland Gavrilescu laid out the company's "autoresearch" framework in a Latent Space interview — a structured approach where AI agents evaluate their own outputs, generate improvement hypotheses, and run experiments to refine their behavior, organized around reusable "recipes" (parameterized agent workflows).

↳ THE REAL STORY
The core mechanism: instead of a human manually tuning prompts or agent logic after each failure, the system runs a feedback loop where the agent itself proposes what went wrong and tests fixes — autoresearch. Recipes act as versioned, composable units of agent behavior, meaning improvements can be isolated, tested, and rolled back like code. For practitioners building multi-step agents today, this is a concrete answer to the "my agent degrades over time" problem — the loop catches drift rather than waiting for a human to notice it in production.
stories.considerations: The human-remains-central framing is doing a lot of work here. Self-improving loops sound autonomous, but every meaningful decision point — what counts as a good output, when to accept a proposed fix, which experiments are worth running — still requires human judgment to define upfront. The risk is that teams adopt the architecture expecting reduced oversight and instead inherit a system that optimizes confidently toward the wrong objective. The real question isn't whether the loop closes, but who defines the reward signal and how often they audit it.

stories.title: How Cursor deploys AI inside the enterprise
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Cursor runs a Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team — led by Pauline Brunet — that embeds directly with enterprise customers to implement agentic coding workflows at the org level, not just hand over a license and walk away.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is less about Cursor the product and more about what enterprise AI adoption actually requires in 2025. The FDE model means Cursor is selling professional services alongside the IDE — helping companies restructure codebases, define agent boundaries, and build what Brunet calls "software factories": repeatable, agent-driven pipelines for shipping code. For a developer or engineering lead evaluating Cursor for a team, this signals that the hard part isn't the tool — it's the organizational plumbing around it. Context management, repo structure, review gates, and prompt conventions all need to be designed before agents add net value at scale.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The FDE model is a classic enterprise wedge — get in, prove value, expand seats. But it also quietly reveals that Cursor's self-serve product isn't sufficient for complex orgs on its own. If you need a dedicated team to make the tool work, that's a real adoption cost that doesn't show up in the per-seat pricing. Worth asking: at what org size does the FDE engagement pay off, and what happens to those workflows when Cursor's underlying models change — which they do, frequently?

stories.title: Warp CEO Zach Lloyd on why software factories are the next phase of coding
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Warp CEO Zach Lloyd is framing the next phase of AI-assisted development not as smarter autocomplete or better agents, but as "software factories" — automated pipelines where code is produced, tested, and iterated at scale with minimal human intervention per task.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The framing matters more than it might seem. Lloyd is essentially arguing that the unit of engineering work shifts from the individual developer writing code to the engineer designing and maintaining the system that writes code. In practice, this means the leverage point moves upstream: the person who defines the factory's constraints, quality gates, and feedback loops becomes more valuable than the person executing individual tickets. For teams building on top of tools like Warp today, this is a signal about where to invest attention — less in prompt engineering individual tasks, more in building repeatable, auditable pipelines with clear success criteria baked in.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The "software factory" metaphor carries an implicit assumption worth stress-testing: that software tasks are modular and parallelizable enough to run on an assembly line. Most mature codebases are not. Shared state, undocumented tribal knowledge, and tangled dependencies are exactly the things that make automated pipelines fail in non-obvious ways. Lloyd is also the CEO of a terminal and developer tooling company with a direct commercial interest in this vision — the factory needs a control room, and Warp wants to be it. That's not disqualifying, but it's worth reading the thesis with that incentive structure in mind.

stories.title: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: Autoresearch and the tension between AI and human agency
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
At the AI Engineer World's Fair, a visible fault line opened between two camps: builders pushing toward fully automated 'software factory' pipelines — where AI agents write, test, and ship code end-to-end — and speakers arguing that removing humans from the loop degrades understanding and erodes meaningful control.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The tension isn't abstract. Autoresearch systems and agentic coding pipelines are already in production at some orgs, compressing the human role to prompt-writer and output-reviewer. The pushback from the stage wasn't philosophical hand-wringing — it was practitioners pointing out that when a system generates code no engineer fully read, debugging becomes archaeology and ownership becomes fiction. For teams evaluating how far to push agentic workflows today, this is the practical question: at what point does velocity gains trade off against the ability to reason about what your system actually does.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The 'software factory' framing assumes the bottleneck is human typing speed. But most engineering failures aren't about how fast code gets written — they're about misunderstood requirements, subtle state bugs, and integration surprises that only surface when a human holds the full context. If agentic pipelines systematically reduce that contextual ownership, the productivity gains may be real in the short term and quietly expensive later. The open question nobody answered at the conference: who is liable when an autonomous pipeline ships a vulnerability nobody read?

stories.title: 🔬 The Coolest Diffusion Research Isn't in LLMs — Evan Feinberg & Sergey Edunov, Genesis Molecular AI
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Sergey Edunov — one of the leads behind Meta's Llama — left to co-found Genesis Molecular AI with Evan Feinberg, focusing on diffusion models applied to drug discovery. The Latent Space episode covers their PEARL system, which won the OpenBind benchmark in zero-shot mode, meaning it predicted protein-ligand binding without task-specific fine-tuning.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The argument here is structural: diffusion model research in molecular biology is roughly where LLM research was in 2020 — the architectures are maturing, the benchmarks are just becoming meaningful, and the people who understand both the ML and the biology are still rare enough to matter. PEARL's zero-shot OpenBind result is the concrete proof point. Co-folding (jointly predicting protein structure and ligand pose) has historically been too inaccurate to use in real drug pipelines; the claim is that Genesis is crossing the threshold where outputs are actually useful to medicinal chemists, not just impressive on paper. For ML practitioners, the interesting technical angle is how diffusion's iterative denoising maps naturally onto conformational sampling — a problem that MD simulations have attacked with brute compute for decades.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
Edunov's departure from Meta is a meaningful signal, but the benchmark to watch critically is the gap between zero-shot leaderboard wins and wet-lab validation. OpenBind measures predicted binding pose accuracy — it does not measure whether a molecule actually binds in an assay, let alone whether it's selective or synthesizable. Every wave of ML-for-drug-discovery has produced models that look strong on structural benchmarks and then stall at experimental confirmation. The honest open question: does Genesis have the biology infrastructure and pharma partnerships to close that loop, or is this still a capabilities demo waiting for a deployment story?
